P64.07.directive: You must submit your written statement within the set deadline after an allegation.
P64.07.why: Grinnell source: 'the statement must be submitted within 3 business days'; a general allegation-procedure deadline.

CT17.c06.directive: You must produce the work you submit yourself; graded code must be written without assistance from AI, and AI tools may not take the place of developing your own solution.
CT17.c06.why: Drexel: 'written by the student without assistance from AI'; Harvey Mudd: 'they may not be used in place of developing a solution' (they = the AI tools).

CT32.c05.directive: You must write your own code and must not copy, share, or submit code you did not write, including code from homework help sites, a TA or generative AI.
CT32.c05.why: Michigan State: 'never submit a code that is not yours even if you received that code from a TA or from any Generative AI'; Memphis names 'homework help' sites.

CT15.c04.directive: You must not use code fragments found through search directly in your solutions.
CT15.c04.why: Wellesley source: 'fragments, you are not allowed to use these directly in your solutions'; about search results, no AI reference.

CT22.c05.directive: You may not upload any files or images to the university's Gemini AI tool.
CT22.c05.why: NC State source: 'No files (or images) are allowed to be uploaded to NCSU Gemini.' Gemini is an AI tool.

CT12.c04.directive: You must not use AI or other writing aids, such as Grammarly, predictive text or translation tools, that revise your sentences or clean up your English.
CT12.c04.why: BYU-Idaho: 'Use AI to clean up your English.' (listed as not allowed); North Texas names Grammarly, predictive text and translation tools; Pomona: 'tools that offer suggested revisions of your sentences'.

CT27.c04.directive: You must not edit, truncate, tamper with, scrub, or regenerate your AI prompts, responses, transcripts or session logs, and you must attest they are complete.
CT27.c04.why: NC State: 'prompts and responses must not be edited or truncated'; UIUC: 'tampering with Claude Code session logs', 'Never ask the AI to reproduce the conversation'.

CT27.c05.directive: Links to AI logs are not accepted as submitted AI transcripts.
CT27.c05.why: Columbia source: 'links to logs are not accepted.' in the context of submitting AI interaction logs.

CT35.c14.directive: You must submit homework as scans of handwritten originals.
CT35.c14.why: Stony Brook source: 'All homework assignments must be submitted as scans of handwritten originals.'; no AI reference.

CT35.c10.directive: If your test answer can be found on the internet, you receive a zero for the test.
CT35.c10.why: Georgia Southern source: 'If your answer to a question can be found on the internet, then your score for the test is zero.'; no AI reference.

CT35.c11.directive: You must not use an IDE on exams and are restricted to a terminal editor.
CT35.c11.why: Rose-Hulman source: 'refrain from using an IDE, and are restricted to' a terminal editor; no AI reference.

CT21.c04.directive: If you have significant programming experience and are working on comprehensive projects, you may generally use AI coding agents.
CT21.c04.why: Loyola Marymount: 'agentic coding is generally acceptable' for experienced students on comprehensive projects; agentic coding is AI coding agents.

CT21.c06.directive: You may set an AI coding agent up on a long task and walk away.
CT21.c06.why: UIUC source: 'setting your agent up on a long task and walking away', in a course built on Claude Code agents.

CT46.c06.directive: You must purchase a Claude Pro AI subscription for the project and should expect two to three months of cost.
CT46.c06.why: UIUC: 'purchase a Claude Pro subscription'; Claude is an AI tool.

CT30.c02.directive: You must understand and be able to explain all code you submit, including everything AI tools suggest; do not copy code you do not understand.
CT30.c02.why: Brown: 'replicate it on your own, without collaboration or AI assistance'; Bucknell: 'Never blindly copy code! You MUST understand everything these tools suggest.'

CT30.c08.directive: You must comment your code to show you understand it and what it does.
CT30.c08.why: Maryland: 'explain the output of any code and comment it'; Texas Tyler: 'Comment on each line of code in the imported method'; neither mentions AI.

CT27.c01.directive: You must include the prompts you used with AI tools, in a file, README, comments, or the hand-in.
CT27.c01.why: Carleton: 'the name and version of the specific LLM you used, as well as the exact prompts'; Brown: 'link to the conversation history or a list of the prompts used'.

CT35.c12.directive: Do exercises in class on your own keyboard, and make-up sessions follow the same rules.
CT35.c12.why: San Francisco source: 'Exercises are done in the room, during the session, on your own keyboard.'; no AI reference.

CT35.c03.directive: You must record your screen during quizzes.
CT35.c03.why: Duke source: 'be asked to record your screen'; no AI reference.

CT35.c17.directive: You must demonstrate your progress to the teaching staff at the end of the assignment.
CT35.c17.why: WPI source: 'demonstrate their progress to the teaching staff at the conclusion of the assignment'; no AI reference.

CT48.c04.directive: You should read the department's supplemental academic integrity policy.
CT48.c04.why: Villanova source: 'review the supplemental academic integrity policy from the computing science department'; no AI reference.

CT40.c12.directive: You must spend time practicing and take responsibility for learning from the work.
CT40.c12.why: UMBC: 'responsibility to learn from this process'; Temple: 'spend time practicing problem solving and writing'; neither mentions AI.

OTHER.c27.directive: You may change flagged parts of your work and resubmit as necessary.
OTHER.c27.why: Washington State source: 'you'll be able to change them and resubmit as necessary'; no AI reference.

CT06.c07.directive: You may tell staff if the AI policy disallows something that should be allowed.
CT06.c07.why: Washington source: 'If you believe the policy disallows something that should be allowed' appears in the course AI policy, so 'the policy' is the AI policy.

P29.01.directive: Make clear that original, personal student work, not AI-generated content, is what counts for assessment.
P29.01.why: smith-college: 'It is the student's voice we want to hear, not the voice of generative AI.'

P117.10.directive: Be cautious of claims that vendors and product providers make about AI tools, and do not assume those tools are safe, secure or private.
P117.10.why: Sources warn about AI tool vendors: michigan-state says tools 'should never be assumed to be safe, secure, or private'.

P33.01.directive: In response to AI, have students complete writing assignments and other coursework in class rather than outside class.
P33.01.why: In-class writing is offered as an AI response strategy (clemson 'in-class/proctored assignments'; baylor 'Require writing to be done in class').

P51.05.directive: Do not replace approved accommodations, such as note-taking accommodations, with AI tools, and do not prohibit approved assistive technologies or accommodations.
P51.05.why: cal-state-long-beach: AI note-taking 'should supplement, not replace' approved accommodations; auburn lists 'Replacing official accommodations'.

P46.04.directive: Review student work yourself rather than leaving grading to AI, and confirm that grades are accurate, consistent and explainable from the student's evidence.
P46.04.why: Sources sit in AI-grading guidance: yeshiva 'Grades and substantive evaluative judgments must be reviewed and confirmed by the instructor of record'.

P33.04.directive: In response to AI, move exams and major assessments to in-person, supervised formats.
P33.04.why: Sources describe in-person assessment as a response to AI (california-berkeley 'this is why I have moved to in-class assessments').

P33.05.directive: You may use lockdown browsers or proctoring tools to keep students from using AI during assessments.
P33.05.why: bowling-green-state: lockdown browser 'to prevent users from using AI assistance'.

P33.06.directive: To limit AI use during exams, you may have students work in front of you or restrict the devices and technology, such as phones and smart wearables, that students can have.
P33.06.why: Device rules target AI-capable devices: georgetown 'recordings and smart wearables', william-and-mary 'restrict the technology tools students can possess'.

P33.09.directive: In response to AI, base at least half of course points on demonstrations of understanding.
P33.09.why: boise-state sets the points rule in its AI assessment redesign: 'at least half of all course points will come from demonstration of understanding'.

P81.10.directive: You may resolve concerns informally or impose an academic sanction under the applicable guidelines.
P81.10.why: General misconduct procedure: nebraska-lincoln 'If misconduct likely happened, you can impose a sanction'; oregon 'resolve academic misconduct concerns informally'.

P93.01.directive: Learn effective AI prompting techniques and teach students to write and refine AI prompts, including through assignments.
P93.01.why: nevada-reno: 'Learn effective AI prompting techniques and experiment with different AI tools.'

P35.02.directive: In response to AI, assess the learning process, through reflection, process documentation and metacognition, not only the final product.
P35.02.why: Assessment redesign for AI: alaska-fairbanks 'embracing AI by modeling good behavior'; boise-state 'rather than initial code creation'.

P35.05.directive: In response to AI, break large assignments into smaller staged parts, such as drafts submitted for feedback.
P35.05.why: Listed as an AI-era redesign strategy (alabama 'submit drafts of their work for review and feedback'; appalachian-state 'scaffolding').

P34.01.directive: In response to AI, build oral explanation or defense of work into assessments.
P34.01.why: Offered as AI-proof assessment (baylor 'Incorporate a verbal exam requirement tied to an essay'; brown 'present and/or explain their' work).

P35.06.directive: In response to AI, design authentic, real-world assessments that require application, analysis and higher-order thinking.
P35.06.why: Authentic assessment is listed as an AI redesign strategy (harvard 'require creativity, practical application of concepts, and critical thinking').

P35.08.directive: In response to AI, use in-class activities, discussion, group work, peer review, presentations and flipped formats so students show learning in person.
P35.08.why: Sources offer in-person work as AI redesign (california-san-diego 'come into class to do activities and demonstrate knowledge and skills').

P35.09.directive: In response to AI, let students submit work in varied formats such as video, audio, podcasts or multimedia instead of only written text.
P35.09.why: AI redesign guidance asks whether writing is the only way to show mastery (appalachian-state; hawaii-manoa 'Replace a writing assignment with an audio file').

P35.10.directive: In response to AI, use frequent low-stakes assessments instead of heavily weighted high-stakes ones.
P35.10.why: AI redesign advice to lower stakes (boise-state 'decrease the weight for projects'; cornell 'Count homework as a relatively small part').

P35.11.directive: In response to AI, require students to cite specific, verifiable sources, including links or DOIs, in their assignments.
P35.11.why: AI guidance on verifying references (illinois-chicago 'verify all information in their writing with peer-reviewed sources'; cornell 'verification of references').

P35.12.directive: Write clear rubrics that reward critical thinking, application and original thought rather than work AI could do.
P35.12.why: cal-state-la: 'rubrics that do not reward work that an AI could do'.

P26.01.directive: Decide and state what documentation of AI use and of their own contributions, such as prompts, AI outputs or drafts, students must keep or submit.
P26.01.why: california-los-angeles: 'how should students document their interactions with GenAI'; georgia-tech 'show their prompts and/or the GenAI output'.

P121.01.directive: Increase human interactions in your courses.
P121.01.why: The only source (new-jersey-institute-technology) says 'increase interactions in their courses' with no AI wording.

P127.01.directive: Offer practical guidance and structures for group work in courses with extensive group projects.
P127.01.why: The only source (massachusetts-institute-technology) says group-project courses 'should offer practical guidance and structures' with no AI wording.

P109.09.directive: Follow the agreed syllabus learning outcomes.
P109.09.why: The only source (northeastern) says faculty 'follow the agreed upon syllabus learning outcomes', a general curricular rule.

P117.09.directive: Research or critically evaluate an AI tool, including its reliability and bias, before choosing it for a class or assignment.
P117.09.why: northeastern 'choosing AI tools carefully'; swarthmore-college 'Critical evaluation of any AI platform'.

P128.01.directive: Decide whether English language learners may write their original drafts in another language.
P128.01.why: The only source (california-santa-cruz) asks whether English language learners may draft in another language, with no AI wording.

P109.06.directive: Develop shared AI syllabus language specific to the discipline or course, so students do not face differing AI rules.
P109.06.why: binghamton: 'difficulty for students, who are trying to navigate AI rules'.

P110.09.directive: If you use the university's provided AI statement, you must include it in the syllabus exactly as written.
P110.09.why: west-virginia's rule concerns its provided AI syllabus statement: 'if a statement is used, it must appear in the syllabus exactly as' written.

P37.01.directive: Decide and set penalty levels for unauthorized AI use, including for first-time and repeat offenders, before the course begins.

P81.01.directive: Learn the reporting and student conduct procedures before misuse occurs.
P81.01.why: General procedure: rutgers 'Become familiar with the student conduct requirements for charging students'.

P95.01.directive: Build a culture of academic integrity in your classroom.
P95.01.why: General integrity norm: vanderbilt 'develop a culture of academic integrity in your classroom'; alabama-birmingham 'Insist on academic integrity.'

P99.04.directive: Normalize struggle in learning and give students many options to get help.
P99.04.why: The only source (harvey-mudd-college) says 'Normalize struggle while learning and provide as many options as possible', with no AI wording.

P66.06.directive: Explain to students the purpose and value of assignments, including how doing the work without AI will help them learn.
P66.06.why: albany: 'how doing work without artificial intelligence will help them learn'.

P117.04.directive: Tell students which tools and resources, AI or otherwise, are reliable sources of information.
P117.04.why: harvey-mudd-college's AI guidance: 'tell students what tools/resources are reliable sources of information', where tools include AI.

P130.01.directive: To know students' own writing apart from AI, collect an in-person or handwritten baseline writing sample early in the course.
P130.01.why: Sources in AI guidance: denver 'get to know your students' writing styles'; seton-hall uses a proctored sample.

P66.07.directive: Discuss academic integrity with students at the start of the course, including how AI fits into it and the difference between plagiarizing with AI and using it as an assistant.
P66.07.why: alaska-fairbanks: 'explain the difference between plagiarizing with AI and using it as an effective assistant'.

P133.01.directive: State in the syllabus or remind students that they are responsible for the work they submit, including any AI-generated content in it.
P133.01.why: florida: 'they are responsible for AI-generated content they submit, present, or publish'.

P111.04.directive: Have students sign a statement acknowledging course expectations at the start.
P111.04.why: General integrity practice: seton-hall 'Have students sign an honor code or statement of understanding'; no AI wording.

P69.01.directive: You should be able to show students knew the course AI rules; departures from stated AI restrictions can be evidence of violations.
P69.01.why: cornell's restrictions are its course AI restrictions: 'deviations from these restrictions could constitute evidence of potential integrity violations'.

P72.02.directive: Remind students of available academic support resources, and be prepared to recognize AI-related academic, social and emotional challenges.
P72.02.why: massachusetts-institute-technology: 'should be prepared to recognize AI-related academic, social, and emotional challenges'.

P99.07.directive: Help students resist the temptation to use AI, discuss what to do if they need help, and give them support from the start.
P99.07.why: albany: 'help them regulate their behavior and the temptation to use AI'.

P40.04.directive: As a check on AI use, you may require students to work on platforms that record version history, such as Google Docs.
P40.04.why: Sources in AI guidance: louisiana-state-new-orleans 'I may ask to see drafts, revision histories, or notes'; massachusetts-institute-technology 'capture a history of versions'.

P34.02.directive: As a check on AI use, check in with students about their process and how they arrive at their work while it is underway.
P34.02.why: AI guidance: michigan-technological 'reserve the right to ask students to explain their process for creating work'.

P35.19.directive: To reduce reliance on AI and other outside resources, use controlled assessment conditions such as timed work, handwriting, in-class exams or randomized questions.
P35.19.why: oberlin-college 'reduce overreliance on electronic resources'; ut-rio-grande-valley 'reduce opportunities to search for answers externally'.

P111.11.directive: Have students affirm an honesty pledge on each assignment or exam.
P111.11.why: General honor-code practice: wesleyan 'sign the Honor Pledge on all assignments and tests'.

P115.11.directive: Consult the conduct or academic integrity office about suspected misuse.
P115.11.why: General procedure: connecticut 'Please consult the UConn Office of Community Standards'.

P81.06.directive: Include evidence, documentation and an explanation of how the student's AI use violated your course policies in your report.
P81.06.why: arkansas-little-rock: 'clearly explain how the student's use of AI violated your course policies'.

P81.08.directive: Submit the required report form within the stated deadline, one per violation.
P81.08.why: Report-form procedure: north-texas 'Use the Academic Violation Report - Single Violation form for EACH violation'.

P81.11.directive: Do not impose your own sanction or grade penalty before the deciding office makes a finding.
P81.11.why: General misconduct procedure: american 'faculty cannot impose any kind of grade penalty based on the suspicion'.

P81.13.directive: Do not discuss the suspected violation with the student or their chair.
P81.13.why: General procedure: grinnell-college 'the instructor should not discuss the case with the student'.

P81.12.directive: Notify the student of the allegation and gather evidence before submitting the report.
P81.12.why: General procedure: washington-state 'Gather the evidence and notify the student of the date and nature of the allegations'.

P57.01.directive: Hold a supportive, non-accusatory conversation with the student before escalating suspected AI misuse.
P57.01.why: Sources discuss conversations about suspected AI use (american 'I'd like to talk to the student about this'; appalachian-state 'collegial and collaborative perspective').

P69.03.directive: When AI misuse is suspected, you may gather drafts, revision histories and process records, such as prompts and AI outputs.
P69.03.why: mercer: 'notes, drafts, source trails, prompts, outputs, or revision histories'; cal-poly-pomona 'original (pre-AI) work'.

P69.08.directive: Review and verify suspected AI cases carefully and objectively, with human analysis, before reporting or taking action.
P69.08.why: virginia-tech: 'requires human analysis of any work being reported as AI plagiarism'.

P69.11.directive: Judge suspected AI misuse using course expectations, assignment requirements, student work and context.
P69.11.why: clark: 'concerns about potential misuse of AI should be evaluated using academic judgment, course context'.

P124.03.directive: Apply academic misconduct enforcement and grading consistently across students, so similar cases receive similar outcomes.
P124.03.why: General enforcement norm: boston 'Apply enforcement policies uniformly to minimize bias'.

P124.05.directive: You must not allow grading practices that conflict with stated integrity requirements.
P124.05.why: General grading rule: clemson 'Allowing grading practices that conflict with stated integrity requirements.'

P40.11.directive: You may reserve the right to review submitted work for AI-generated content at any later point.
P40.11.why: william-and-mary: 'submitted work may always be reviewed, as needed, for AI-generated content'.

P34.08.directive: In response to AI, oral examinations and code reviews are growing practices for checking that students understand their submitted work.
P34.08.why: Sources in AI guidance: brown 'increasing use of oral examinations'; northeastern 'code reviews that require students to show they understand'.

CT27.c08.directive: You may ask students for their AI prompt transcripts.
CT27.c08.why: georgia-tech's course AI policy: 'the instructional team reserves the right to ask' for prompt transcripts, which are AI records.

CT39.c04.directive: You may talk with the student about suspected AI misuse before any report.
CT39.c04.why: wellesley-college's course AI policy: 'we may, at any point in the semester, have a' conversation with the student.

CT39.c06.directive: Reporting students for AI cheating is exhausting for the instructor.
CT39.c06.why: washington: 'the use of AI tools requires time and energy, and is emotionally' draining; yale 'too exhausting ... to keep reporting'.

P72.01.directive: Provide students and advisors with contact information for human assistance, a list of campus resources and a designated referral point for help with AI, such as a peer program run by students with AI skills.
P72.01.why: The sources sit in AI guidance and one names AI directly ('a peer-to-peer program for students that taps into students with AI skill sets'); 'human assistance' is offered as the human alternative to AI help.

P139.01.directive: Adopt and apply the AI guidance and points to consider that the university recommends, for example to make AI cheating less necessary and less appealing.
P139.01.why: The guidance being adopted is the AI guidance itself: Lehigh says it should 'make AI "cheating" both less necessary and less appealing'; Pittsburgh and USC refer to their AI recommendations.

P69.09.directive: Findings of AI-related misconduct require a standard of proof, such as clear and convincing evidence or more likely than not, that AI or other unauthorized aid was used.
P69.09.why: William & Mary applies the standard to 'whether AI has been used to reach the threshold of proof', and UC Irvine to whether 'you did not personally complete an assignment', in AI guidance.

P69.15.directive: The burden of proof in academic misconduct cases lies with the university.
P69.15.why: Both sources state a general rule for all misconduct cases ('The burden of proof is on the university for all academic misconduct cases'), with no AI-specific content.

P71.06.directive: Provide channels for reporting concerns and AI-related ethical violations, correcting errors and seeking redress, and receive and review the reports.
P71.06.why: North Florida names the object: 'mechanisms for reporting and addressing AI-related ethical violations'; the other sources describe the same channels in AI governance documents.

P71.07.directive: Activate incident response for AI-related security incidents, document and investigate them, notify affected parties and regulators, and refer violations to proper bodies.
P71.07.why: Virginia Tech's source is 'Incident Response: AI-related security incident procedures'; the others describe the incident procedure in the same AI governance documents.

P60.06.directive: Ensure students do not feel policed.
P60.06.why: The only source says 'Students should not feel policed.' and names no AI tool, detector or AI-specific practice.

P68.09.directive: Develop and deploy educational modules to help students who commit violations.
P68.09.why: The source ('Educational modules should be developed and deployed to assist students with violations') concerns integrity violations in general and does not mention AI.

P137.03.directive: Retain applicable records and then destroy them in accordance with the state's records retention requirements.
P137.03.why: The source restates the state's general records rule ('Applicable records must be retained and then destroyed in accordance with the Commonwealth's Records Retention'), with nothing AI-specific.

P54.12.directive: If you serve on a designated body, recommend revisions or updates to the AI policy as legal, technological and regulatory requirements change.
P54.12.why: Purdue's source is 'Provide recommendations on policy changes regarding the use of AI'; Augusta and Santa Monica tie updates to 'updated regulatory requirements' and 'legal, technological, and regulatory developments'.

P99.12.directive: Most students who violate integrity rules do so out of stress, anxiety and academic pressure.
P99.12.why: The sources describe why students cheat in general ('Most students who commit violations do it out of stress'), not anything about AI.

CT09.c05.directive: Only course staff may provide solution-specific debugging assistance.
CT09.c05.why: The source ('Only the course staff may provide solution-specific debugging assistance.') is a general collaboration rule that names no AI tool.

CT38.c07.directive: You may review students' AI session transcripts.
CT38.c07.why: The source 'Staff may review transcripts' refers to the transcripts of students' AI chat sessions that the course's AI policy discusses.

P86.11.directive: When AI records or transcribes a meeting, balance productivity and convenience with respect for all participants' privacy, and treat the recordings as private among those who took part.
P86.11.why: Both Davidson sentences come from its guidance on AI meeting recording and transcription; 'productivity and convenience' is the benefit of those AI tools and 'considered private among those who participated' refers to their recordings.

P93.06.directive: Structure your AI prompts with elements such as a role or persona, task, context and format.
P93.06.why: The sources are about prompting AI: 'When writing an AI prompt, focus on persona, task, context and format' (Sam Houston State) and 'Assign a role to ChatGPT' (Santa Clara).

P93.13.directive: Learn prompt engineering for AI tools, including how to write clear, precise and iterative prompts that work.
P93.13.why: Prompt engineering is a skill for AI tools, and the sources say so ('Learning to use AI responsibly and ethically is an important skill', Pepperdine; 'clear, precise, and iterative prompts', North Dakota State).

P76.05.directive: Follow university communications standards and approval processes for public-facing and official materials made or edited with AI, such as photos.
P76.05.why: Buffalo's source applies the standards to 'Photos created or edited using AI for official UB purposes'; the others apply existing communications rules within AI guidance.

P117.07.directive: Verify that an AI tool has adequate security, such as encryption and secure data handling, and is appropriate for your data before using it.
P117.07.why: The sources describe checking the AI tools the guidance covers: 'Ensure the tool has robust security measures in place, such as encryption' (UNLV) and 'verify that the specific tool you are using is appropriate for your data' (Utah State).

P75.03.directive: Report suspicious messages and communications, and questionable AI output, to the designated IT or security office.
P75.03.why: Colby's source names AI: 'Report suspicious communications and questionable AI output to ITS.'; the others repeat the reporting duty inside AI guidance on phishing.

P71.10.directive: If you do research, report adverse events or unanticipated problems to the IRB.
P71.10.why: The source ('Researchers must report any adverse events or unanticipated problems to the IRB') is the general IRB reporting rule and does not mention AI.

P114.03.directive: If you are not linked to the university and cause damage through AI use, you alone answer for it, exonerating the university, and you are barred from using AI technology there.
P114.03.why: The source ('responderá exclusivamente por el daño causado , eximiendo y exonerando a la') is in the university's AI policy, and 'the technology' the person is barred from is the AI technology that policy governs.

P80.08.directive: Escalate denials, disputes and unresolved questions about AI use to a named committee, such as an AI governance committee, or to a leader or program head.
P80.08.why: Arkansas sends appeals to 'the AI Governance Committee' and Delaware asks people to raise questions 'as they pertain to the use of Generative AI'.

P52.16.directive: You keep ownership of your own prompts, work and course materials when you use AI tools.
P52.16.why: The sources are about AI tools: 'the person entering the prompts and text materials retains the copyright' (UAB) and 'your content is not used to train any models, and you retain ownership' (Portland CC).

CT02.c11.directive: Appropriate use of technology as an aid for learning counts as academic honesty.
CT02.c11.why: The source ('includes the appropriate use of technology as an aid for learning and productivity') is a general honesty statement about technology and does not mention AI.
